visual.title: Four-layer microbiome measurement ladder
visual.description: A step sequence that separates the four things a microbiome claim can rest on, abundance, viability, activity and clinical outcome, then places the study types that can measure each layer and the claims usually made from the lowest one.
steps: Step 1, layer one, abundance: write sequencing-based composition, and note the caveat that genetic material can be detected without the organism being alive.
Step 2, layer two, viability: write culture-based methods, and note that these detect only organisms able to grow under laboratory conditions.
Step 3, layer three, activity: write functional or metabolite measurements, and note that activity is rarely reported in cosmetic studies even when composition is.
Step 4, layer four, clinical outcome: write the skin endpoint that actually matters, such as fewer flares or better comfort, and mark it as the layer almost never reaching the claim.

Step 5, claim comparison: place a marketing phrase such as restores a healthy microbiome beside the lowest layer and draw a dashed arrow upward, labelling it an inference not yet made in the studies available.

Step 6, habitat note: annotate the ladder with the interventions that do have evidence across all four layers, gentle cleansing, consistent moisturising and photoprotection, and note that these support the habitat rather than installing a specified community.

lessons.title: Capstone: one dossier, one decision rule set, one honest limit
lessons.explanation: This lesson assembles the whole level into a single deliverable that a learner can produce in an afternoon and use for a year: an evidence dossier for one real product question, ending in a decision rule with a stop rule, a cost line and an explicit referral map. The method has five parts. Part one is the question. Write it as a sentence with four slots: the person and their actual constraint, the intervention, the comparison and the outcome that would count, for example for a reactive skin on the cheeks, would a ceramide moisturiser reduce stinging episodes over eight weeks compared with the current plain emollient. The comparison slot is the one most often left empty, and leaving it empty is what turns a dossier into shopping. Part two is the ladder of sources, assembled in a fixed order: regulatory and clinical guidance first, then systematic reviews with a stated risk-of-bias assessment, then randomised trials, then observational studies, then manufacturer material, with the manufacturer material labelled as promotional even when it contains data. The Cochrane risk-of-bias domains give the appraisal template for the trial rung, and the ROBIS and AMSTAR-2 instruments are the review-level equivalents, which is why the dermatology review-quality study cited in lesson 64 exists at all. Part three is extraction into a table with fixed columns: design, participants, duration, outcome and its measurement, effect and precision, funding and declared interests, and the appraisal note. Extraction is where most claims collapse, because a claim that has a duration, a comparator and a precision can be weighed, and a claim that has none of the three cannot. Part four is the certainty label. Use three plain-language labels with written criteria rather than adjectives. Likely means at least one randomised comparison with a relevant outcome and no serious risk-of-bias problem. Uncertain means randomised evidence exists but is small, short, inconsistent or indirectly relevant. Insufficient means no randomised comparison addresses the endpoint, which is the correct label for most microbiome and growth-factor claims and not a synonym for false. Part five is the decision rule: what you will do, what you will stop, what you will measure, over what interval, and what will make you stop early. The stop rule is the part that protects the learner, and it has two forms: a tolerance stop, meaning irritation, stinging or new scaling that persists beyond a few days, and a clinical stop, meaning any symptom that belongs to a clinician. The Federal Trade Commission framework is useful here as a consumer instrument rather than only a business rule, because it establishes that advertisers must have adequate substantiation for objective claims before dissemination and that health-related claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence, so asking a brand for the study behind a claim is a legitimate request with a defined standard behind it. The referral map is the final element and it draws on the whole course. It should name, in writing, the triggers for a dermatologist for a changing or non-healing lesion, a persistent rash, a suspected contact allergy that needs patch testing, and scarring or pigment change that is worsening, and, separately, the triggers for an eye-care clinician for anything involving the lid margin, the lashes or the ocular surface, plus the red flags of new eye pain, light sensitivity, discharge, persistent redness or any change in vision. For this course's learner, who lives with a diagnosed corneal condition and impaired vision, that second list is not a formality; it is the part of the dossier that should never be written from a label. The dossier is education, not individualized medical advice, and its proper output is a set of well-formed questions and a documented plan rather than a diagnosis.
lessons.example: Worked example with arithmetic, start to finish. The question is whether to switch from a plain emollient to a ceramide-containing moisturiser for the cheeks, given recurrent stinging. Step one, find the evidence. Regulatory and clinical guidance supports moisturising for dry and reactive skin without preferring one formulation. Systematic reviews of moisturiser composition have inconsistent endpoints, so a search results in two reviews: one pooling within-group hydration changes that support moisturising in general, and one pooling randomised comparisons against plain emollients that is inconclusive for the ceramide question. Assign labels: likely that moisturising helps dryness, insufficient that ceramides beat a plain emollient for stinging. Step two, extract what exists. A randomised trial of the specific product reports 60 participants, eight weeks, investigator-rated erythema and participant-rated stinging, with a plain emollient comparator, funded by the manufacturer. Record the comparator and the funding, because generous comparators and interested funders change how a small trial should be weighted. Step three, do the arithmetic on change. If stinging was rated 3.1 out of 10 at baseline in the ceramide group and 2.4 at eight weeks, the change is 0.7 points, and if the control group moved from 3.0 to 2.7 the between-group difference is 0.4 points. On a ten-point scale with self-reported stinging, 0.4 points is smaller than the day-to-day variation most people experience, so the honest reading is a possible small benefit rather than a reason to switch. Step four, do the arithmetic on cost, because a routine has to survive a budget. Product A costs 48 dollars for 30 millilitres, which is 1.60 dollars per millilitre. At 0.5 millilitres twice daily the annual volume is 365 millilitres, which is 12.2 bottles, or about 584 dollars a year. Product B costs 22 dollars for 50 millilitres, which is 0.44 dollars per millilitre, giving about 7.3 bottles and 161 dollars a year. The difference is about 423 dollars a year. Step five, write the decision rule. Given insufficient evidence for the stinging endpoint, possible-scale differences below measurement variation, and a 423-dollar annual gap, the rule is to stay on the current emollient for eight weeks, record stinging episodes in a two-line daily note, spend nothing, and revisit the dossier if episodes fall by half on their own, because that outcome would mean the original variable was not the moisturiser. Stop early for any new scaling, oozing or spreading. Take the note to a clinician if the stinging is accompanied by swelling or blistering, since that is a patch-testing question rather than a product question. Step six, write the limit. This dossier answers a comparison question about two products for one person's reported symptom and does not diagnose the cause of stinging; if a clinician has already given a diagnosis, that diagnosis and its management take precedence over anything in the dossier.
lessons.question: A learner finishes a dossier and finds that the only study of her product question is a single-arm, 20-participant, four-week study published by the manufacturer. What is the correct certainty label and the correct next action?
lessons.answer: Insufficient, because no randomised comparison addresses the endpoint, so the plan should continue the current routine, record the symptom, set a review date, and treat any diagnostic question as a clinical referral rather than a reason to buy
lessons.distractor: Likely, because a published study exists with a measured outcome, and a dossier with any evidence at all is stronger than no dossier
lessons.correction: The labels have written criteria rather than adjectives. Likely requires at least one randomised comparison with a relevant outcome and no serious risk-of-bias problem; a single-arm manufacturer study has no comparator, cannot separate regression to the mean or changed behaviour, and its funding is relevant to how much weight it carries. Insufficient does not mean false, it means the evidence cannot answer the question. The correct plan is to continue the current routine, measure the symptom honestly, set a review date, and route any diagnostic question to the appropriate clinician, which is a stronger position than switching products on the strength of one uncontrolled study.

depth.definitions: Dossier: a written record of a question, the sources appraised, the extracted data, a certainty label and a decision rule. PICO-style question: a question framed by population, intervention, comparison and outcome. Certainty label: a plain-language rating of confidence in an answer, used here as likely, uncertain or insufficient with written criteria. Stop rule: a pre-committed condition for ending a trial of a product, covering both tolerance and clinical triggers. Referral map: a written list of symptoms and situations that route to a clinician rather than to a product decision. Substantiation: evidence sufficient to support an advertising claim, which the Federal Trade Commission requires before dissemination for objective and health-related claims. Confidence interval: the range of values compatible with the observed data. Precision: how narrow that range is.
depth.mechanism: A dossier works because it fixes the question and the criteria before the evidence is gathered, which prevents the common pattern of deciding first and collecting support afterwards. Fixing the outcome slot in advance also prevents the substitution of an easier outcome later: a learner who wants fewer stinging episodes but ends up reporting that skin feels smoother has changed the question rather than answered it. The certainty labels work by separating three different problems that all produce an inconclusive answer, namely no study, a study with the wrong endpoint, and studies that disagree, because each has a different next action. The cost line works by making the decision comparable on a per-year basis rather than per bottle, which is the only unit in which two differently sized products can be compared. The referral map works as a pre-commitment device, because the moment a symptom appears is the worst moment to decide whether it is serious, and having written it earlier makes the decision a rule rather than a judgement made under discomfort.
depth.secondExample: Run the same five-part method on a question where the answer is yes. A learner with cracked, painful hands from frequent washing asks whether switching to an occlusive ointment at night reduces cracking. Guidance and clinical literature support occlusive moisturising for hand dermatitis and identify wet work as a major risk factor, so the guidance rung is favourable rather than merely neutral. A Cochrane review of interventions to prevent occupational irritant hand dermatitis provides the review rung with a stated risk-of-bias assessment, and its conclusions speak to prevention in a working population. Extraction is straightforward because the outcome, cracking and pain, is clinically meaningful and measurable, and the comparator, continuing a lotion, is realistic. Assign likely, because a review with relevant outcomes supports the direction and the mechanism, occlusion improving barrier recovery, is not contested. The decision rule then becomes concrete: ointment at night for four weeks, count bleeding cracks per week, and continue or stop on the count rather than on feel. Note that the same method produced insufficient for the ceramide question and likely for this one. A dossier that labels everything uncertain is as unhelpful as one that labels everything likely, and differentiating between questions is the demonstration that the method is working.
depth.mistake: The most common failure is a dossier that becomes a purchase justification: the question is written after the decision, the outcome slot is filled in with whatever the product measured, and the certainty label is chosen to match the amount spent. A second failure is the opposite, an evaluation so sceptical that every intervention is labelled unproven, which leaves no plan and no way to learn from experience. A third failure is to omit the limit, so that a comparison between two products quietly turns into a diagnostic claim about why the skin is reacting. The diagnostic correction is a single check performed at the end: read the question sentence aloud and ask whether the outcome in it is the outcome the evidence measured, whether the comparison is the one that matters, and whether any sentence in the dossier would change meaning if the learner were sitting in a clinician's office. Any sentence that would gain authority there does not belong in the dossier.
depth.application: Capstone task. Produce a one-page dossier with seven labelled sections: question with population, intervention, comparison and outcome; sources with a rung label and an appraisal note for each; an extraction table with design, participants, duration, outcome and measurement, effect with precision, and funding; a certainty label with the criterion that produced it; a cost line computed per year at a stated application volume; a decision rule with a tolerance stop and a clinical stop; and a referral map with one dermatology trigger and one eye-care trigger. Model response and self-review rubric: a complete dossier names the comparison explicitly, converts every percentage into the scale it came from, shows its annual arithmetic with units, labels manufacturer material as promotional, states what would change the decision and when it will be reviewed, and routes anything touching the lid margin, lashes or ocular surface to an eye-care clinician rather than to a product choice. A dossier with no cost line, no stop rule or no referral map is incomplete regardless of how many studies it cites.
depth.summary: The capstone converts a level of appraisal skills into one durable artefact. Five parts, a four-slot question, a ranked source ladder with rung labels, a fixed extraction table, three criteria-based certainty labels, and a decision rule with a cost line and both a tolerance and a clinical stop, produce an answer that can be reviewed rather than merely believed. The referral map keeps the boundary explicit: a changing or non-healing lesion, a persistent rash or a suspected contact allergy goes to a dermatologist, and anything touching the lid margin, the lashes or the ocular surface goes to an eye-care clinician. The dossier's honest limit is that it compares products and organises questions; it does not diagnose, and it does not replace clinical care.

readings.title: US Federal Trade Commission, Health Products Compliance Guidance (ftc.gov) - the introduction and the section on substantiation
readings.note: Read the two principles stated near the start and the passage requiring competent and reliable scientific evidence for health-related claims. Read it as a consumer instrument: it defines the standard a brand must meet before making a claim, which is what makes a request for the underlying study reasonable rather than impertinent.

readings.title: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, Chapter 8: Assessing risk of bias in a randomized trial (training.cochrane.org)
readings.note: Use the five bias domains as the appraisal template for the trial rung of the dossier: randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Read the domain descriptions once, then use them as the checklist column in your extraction table.

readings.title: Joshi et al. (2024), Quality of systematic reviews and meta-analyses in dermatology, Cochrane Evidence Synthesis and Methods (PMC11795973) - Methods
readings.note: Read the methods for how ROBIS and AMSTAR-2 are applied to reviews, which is the review rung equivalent of the trial appraisal template. Use it to justify labelling a review as appraised or unappraised in your dossier rather than simply counting the number of reviews found.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, Rash 101 in adults: When to seek medical treatment (aad.org)
readings.note: Read the list for the dermatology side of the referral map, namely the situations in which a rash should be assessed by a clinician rather than treated cosmetically. Use it to write concrete triggers rather than a general note to see a doctor if worried, and pair it with the eye-care triggers from lesson 65.

visual.title: One-page dossier template with decision and referral branches
visual.description: A step sequence that lays out the seven sections of the capstone dossier in order and shows where the certainty label, the cost line and the two referral branches attach to the decision.
steps: Step 1, question box: write population, intervention, comparison and outcome in four labelled slots, and strike out the dossier if the comparison slot is empty.

Step 2, source ladder: draw five rungs labelled regulatory and clinical guidance, systematic reviews with bias assessment, randomised trials, observational studies, manufacturer material, and note the appraisal template used at each rung.
Step 3, extraction table: draw columns for design, participants, duration, outcome and measurement, effect with precision, funding and interests, and appraisal note, then enter one row per source.
Step 4, certainty label: draw three boxes labelled likely, uncertain and insufficient, write the criterion under each, and draw an arrow from the extraction table to exactly one box.

Step 5, decision and cost: draw a box containing what will be done, the annual cost computed at a stated volume in millilitres per day, the outcome to be counted, the review date, and the tolerance stop rule.

Step 6, referral branches: draw two arrows leaving the decision box, one labelled dermatology triggers for a changing lesion, a persistent rash or suspected contact allergy needing patch testing, the other labelled eye-care triggers for anything at the lid margin, lashes or ocular surface, plus new pain, light sensitivity, discharge or vision change.

questions.prompt: A learner compares an ointment that improves measured hydration and a lotion that she will actually apply twice daily. Which formulation judgement follows from the vehicle evidence?
questions.answer: Occlusion improves hydration, penetration and contact time while making a product greasier and harder to spread, so vehicle choice depends on site, washes per day and whether the product will be used consistently
questions.distractor: The ointment is better because greater occlusion always delivers more of the active, so tolerability is only a cosmetic preference
questions.correction: The vehicle review sets out both sides of the same trade-off: occlusive ointments increase hydration, penetration and efficacy, resist water and need fewer preservatives, but are greasy, hard to wash off and harder to spread than creams, lotions and gels. Delivery is also bounded, since the 56-compound penetration study found delivery between 0.03 and 72.61 micrograms per square centimetre, with even the highest value well under one per cent of the applied dose. A product that is not used consistently delivers nothing, so tolerability is a delivery variable rather than a preference.

questions.prompt: A learner with eyelid dermatitis reads that methylisothiazolinone reacted in 12.2 per cent of patch-tested patients while paraben mix reacted in 1 per cent, and decides to buy paraben-free products. Two of the replacements are preserved with isothiazolinones. What is the best analysis?
questions.answer: The substitution moves her toward the more frequently sensitising preservative in the dataset, so the change is not automatically safer; identifying her own sensitisers requires clinical patch testing rather than label avoidance
questions.distractor: Buying paraben-free is still the safer choice because parabens carry a hazard signal while the replacement preservatives carry none
questions.correction: The patch-test data do not support that ranking. In the 50,799-patient series, 22.3 per cent reacted to at least one preservative, methylisothiazolinone at 12.2 per cent was the most frequent, and paraben mix at 1 per cent sat near the bottom, a twelvefold difference. The eyelid is a high-risk site for contact dermatitis, with preservatives among the top allergen groups in a 215-patient periorbital series. Hazard is a property of a substance, while personal risk depends on her own sensitisation, so patch testing is the step that produces an answer and a free-from label does not.

questions.prompt: A peptide serum claims to relax expression lines through a muscle-relaxing mechanism, and cites a 45-participant study showing reduced wrinkle depth over eight weeks. What is the correct appraisal?
questions.answer: The outcome and the mechanism are separate claims: the peptide is described as hydrophilic and relatively large with limited stratum corneum permeability, so dermal delivery is challenging and the neuromuscular claim remains uncertain even if a wrinkle measurement improved
questions.distractor: Because a controlled study showed reduced wrinkle depth, the muscle-relaxing mechanism is confirmed and the product works as described
questions.correction: The acetyl hexapeptide-8 review states that the molecule faces limited permeability through the lipophilic stratum corneum, that dermal delivery is challenging, and that the ability to reach neuromuscular junctions remains uncertain, while allowing that studies suggest improvements in wrinkle depth, elasticity and hydration whose mechanisms are incompletely understood. One measured endpoint does not validate a different mechanism, and a wrinkle-scale change also needs to exceed the error of the rating method to be meaningful. The honest filing is outcome unverified and mechanism unproven.

questions.prompt: A prebiotic serum reports a significant change in bacterial composition at four weeks in a single-arm study of 18 participants, and the brand states that it restores a healthy microbiome. What is the strongest appraisal?
questions.answer: Composition, viability, activity and clinical outcome are four different measurements, and evidence for microbiome-targeted cosmetics remains preliminary, so a compositional change in a small single-arm study does not establish restoration or benefit
questions.distractor: Because the study found a statistically significant compositional change, the product alters the microbiome as claimed and skin health should follow
questions.correction: The review literature describes the microbiome as maintaining barrier function and homeostasis, states that dysbiosis is associated with inflammatory conditions, and then states that evidence for microbiome-targeted cosmetics remains preliminary; microbiome-friendly describes a design intention. A compositional change reports what genetic material was present rather than what was alive, active or beneficial, and a single-arm design cannot exclude changed cleansing habits, season or attention effects. The defensible conclusion is that the claim is unverified, while gentle cleansing, moisturising and photoprotection carry the better evidence.

questions.prompt: A learner's dossier contains eight sources, a question and a decision, but no cost line, no stop rule and no referral note. A friend says it is a complete dossier because the evidence is extensive. What is the correct assessment?
questions.answer: It is incomplete: a dossier without a comparison, a certainty label with criteria, an annual cost line, a tolerance stop rule and a written referral map cannot support a decision that can be reviewed rather than merely believed
questions.distractor: It is complete because the number of sources is the measure of an evidence dossier, and a decision follows once the evidence has been gathered
questions.correction: The dossier template has seven sections because each fixes something that would otherwise be decided afterwards. Without a stated comparison the question becomes shopping, without a certainty label with written criteria the confidence level is chosen to match the decision already made, without an annual cost line products of different sizes cannot be compared, and without stop and referral rules the decision is made at the worst moment, while a symptom is present. The referral map keeps the clinical boundary visible, in particular for anything at the lid margin, lashes or ocular surface with a diagnosed corneal condition.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A brand presents a barrier claim as follows: trans-epidermal water loss fell 22 per cent in a four-week study of 28 participants using the product, measured on the forearm with an open-chamber device, and the same product is recommended on its website for use around the eyes. A learner with reactive cheeks and a diagnosed corneal condition asks whether to buy it. Build the appraisal in the order this level teaches, naming the site, the instrument, the design and the boundary. State what the 22 per cent does and does not establish, and state what you would do about the eye-area recommendation.
questions.answer: First, the site: forearm evidence is evidence about the forearm, and the eyelid is the thinnest skin on the body at 0.55 mm with easier allergen penetration, so the eye-area recommendation is unsupported by the study. Second, the instrument: a 22 per cent fall in a water-loss rate needs the site's reliability and the method's measurement error, and forearm TEWL reliability has been reported anywhere from 0.74 to 0.4. Third, the design: a single-arm four-week study cannot separate product effect from regression to the mean, seasonal humidity change or altered routine. Fourth, the boundary: anything at the lid margin, lashes or ocular surface with a diagnosed corneal condition belongs to an eye-care clinician, so the eye recommendation is a clinical question, while the cheek question continues as a monitored trial with a stop rule.
questions.distractor: The study is adequate for both uses because it measured a physiologically relevant endpoint at a relevant duration in 28 participants, and the eye-area recommendation follows from the product being the same formula; the only remaining caveat is that 28 participants is a small sample.
questions.correction: Sample size is the least of the problems. A forearm water-loss measurement does not transfer to the periorbital region, whose skin is the thinnest on the body and whose allergen profile differs; a rate change of 22 per cent is uninterpretable without the site reliability and the measurement error of the device, given that forearm reliability has been reported as low as 0.4; and a single-arm before-and-after design cannot attribute the change to the product. The eye-area claim is not a cosmetic claim that a learner can test, because decisions at the lid margin and ocular surface belong to an eye-care clinician, and this is especially so with a diagnosed corneal condition. The correct output is a cheek-level trial with a written stop rule, and a set of questions for the clinician about the eye area.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. Two colleagues present evidence for the same barrier cream. Colleague one cites a study in which capacitance readings rose from 42 to 51 arbitrary units after eight weeks in a single treated group. Colleague two cites a regional measurement study reporting that TEWL reliability ranges from 0.74 to 0.4 across sites while capacitance reliability was above 0.75 everywhere. Colleague one concludes the cream works and colleague two says the number cannot be interpreted. Using instrument and design reasoning, adjudicate, and include the arithmetic that converts the change into units and compares it with an illustrative measurement error.
questions.answer: Both are partly right and the reasoning is separable. The arithmetic is a change of 9 units on a baseline of 42, which is 21 per cent, so the percentage is reported correctly. The design is a single-arm before-and-after comparison, which cannot exclude regression to the mean, season, humidity or changed behaviour. The measurement point is that capacitance is the more reliable of the two methods in the cited study, with reliability above 0.75 at every site, but reliability below 1 still implies error: if the between-person standard deviation were 12 units, a reliability of 0.75 gives a measurement error of 12 multiplied by the square root of 0.25, which is 6 units. A 9-unit change is larger than a 6-unit error, so it is plausible and modest rather than established, and a between-group comparison of the same size would be substantially stronger evidence.
questions.distractor: Colleague one is correct because the change exceeds the measurement error and the reported reliability was good, so the cream works; colleague two is confusing instrument error with study design, which are independent topics.
questions.correction: The change does exceed an illustrative measurement error, which is why the claim is not dismissed, but exceeding error is not the same as establishing causation. Reliability above 0.75 still leaves appreciable error, and the calculation shows the effect and the error are of the same order, which is a modest result. More importantly, the arithmetic cannot repair the design: a single-arm change over eight weeks is compatible with regression to the mean, seasonal and humidity change, and the behaviour change that accompanies starting a new product. The two objections are additive rather than separate, since error limits what a study can detect while design limits what a detected difference can be attributed to.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A cosmetic trial reports that 60 participants were randomised to active or vehicle, that 48 completed, and that the active group improved significantly in the per-protocol analysis of completers. The abstract says the treatment was proven effective. Identify the specific reporting and analysis problems, state what the intention-to-treat analysis would require, and name the two checklist items a reader should look for that this summary omits.
questions.answer: The problems are analysis population and reporting. Analysing only the 48 completers breaks the comparison randomisation created, because non-completion is related to tolerability and motivation; the CONSORT authors replaced the phrase intention to treat with an explicit request for information about retaining participants in their originally assigned groups precisely because that term is misused. An intention-to-treat analysis requires outcomes for every randomised participant, analysed in the assigned group, with any missing data handled by a stated method. The two omitted checklist items are how the allocation sequence was concealed from recruiters and who was blinded to what, including whether the outcome assessor was blinded. Proven effective is also an overstatement of a result measured on a self-reported or investigator-rated scale in a single trial.
questions.distractor: The main problem is the small sample and the 20 per cent loss to follow-up; once the trial is large enough, restricting analysis to completers is a legitimate way to improve data quality, and the abstract wording is a minor style issue.
questions.correction: Non-completion is not random noise to be trimmed away. Removing it selects a more tolerant, more motivated subgroup, which can manufacture a benefit that would not appear in the full randomised population, and the per-protocol result is therefore the one most vulnerable to bias rather than the cleanest. The intention-to-treat principle exists to preserve the property randomisation created, and the reporting standard asks explicitly about retention in assigned groups. Sample size and attrition matter, but they compound these problems rather than replacing them, and dismissing the abstract wording ignores that abstract claims are what most readers actually carry away.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A 40-participant split-face trial finds no significant difference between the treated and control sides at twelve weeks, and the brand argues that the null result nevertheless shows the design was rigorous. A sceptical reader argues the null result proves the product does not work. Using the design logic from this level, state the correct interpretation and explain what further information would change the conclusion.
questions.answer: Neither argument is sound. A split-face design is efficient because it removes between-person variance, which raises the information per participant, but it assumes the two sides are independent: if product migrates across the midline or if treatment produces a shared systemic effect, the observed difference is diluted toward zero. A null split-face result can therefore reflect either no effect or a design that suppressed the effect, and a design cannot be validated by its own null result. What would change the conclusion is a reported effect size with its precision, an appropriately blinded assessor, cross-midline migration accounted for, and a parallel-group or independent-site comparison, since a null result in a design capable of detecting the expected difference would be substantially more informative.
questions.distractor: Because the trial was randomised, blinded and split-face, the null result is definitive: a rigorous design that finds nothing means the product has no effect, and the sceptical reader is correct.
questions.correction: Rigour describes how well a design removes alternative explanations for a positive result, not how sensitive it is to a true effect in the negative direction. Split-face designs gain efficiency by subtracting between-person variance but assume independence of the two sides, and cross-contamination or shared systemic effects reduce the measured difference, biasing the estimate toward the null rather than away from it. The asymmetric consequence is important: a positive split-face result is relatively conservative, while a null one is ambiguous. Precision, blinding of the assessor and confirmation with an independent-site or parallel design are what would license the conclusion that the product does not work.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A learner finds three sources on one question: a manufacturer summary reporting a 30 per cent wrinkle improvement, a network meta-analysis ranking retinoids highest among topical agents with a stated safety caveat, and a systematic review noting spin in abstracts of dermatology meta-analyses. Explain how to weigh the three, what the 30 per cent needs before it can be compared with the network meta-analysis, and what the spin study changes about how the learner should read the other two.
questions.answer: Weigh them by question and method, not by number. The manufacturer summary is promotional material, so it is labelled as such and it reports a relative change whose scale, comparator, duration and precision must be recovered before any comparison: 30 per cent of a nine-point baseline of 5.0 is 1.6 points, which is meaningful only if it came from a randomised blinded comparison that exceeded the error of the rating scale. The network meta-analysis answers a different question, namely the comparative ranking of topical interventions across 23 randomised trials and 3,905 participants, and it carries its own limitation, since ranking through indirect comparisons assumes that vehicles, concentrations, populations and durations are similar enough to combine. The spin study changes reading habits rather than conclusions: it shows that abstracts can misrepresent results, so the learner reads the results and limitations sections for the primary outcome rather than trusting the abstract, and treats favourable framing as a reason to check, not as evidence.
questions.distractor: The network meta-analysis is the strongest source and should simply be preferred, and since it is a synthesis rather than a manufacturer document, the spin finding applies only to industry-funded material and can be set aside.
questions.correction: Preferring a source by type alone repeats the error the level is designed to correct. The meta-analysis ranks interventions it did not test directly, so its ordering depends on network assumptions, and its safety caveat matters as much as its efficacy ranking for a reactive-skin learner. The manufacturer summary is not worthless, but it is promotional, and its relative percentage must be converted to the study scale and compared with measurement error and with a control condition. Spin is a property of how results are reported, and it has been documented in systematic reviews and meta-analyses in dermatology as well as in randomised trials, so it is a reason to read results sections in every source, including a synthesis.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A learner with a diagnosed corneal condition and impaired vision wants to try a new under-eye cream marketed as ophthalmologist tested, and asks whether she should also resume applying eyeliner at the inner lash line because a video showed it makes eyes look larger. Using the periorbital evidence, answer both parts, name the mechanism by which the eyeliner change matters, and state the stop rule that should accompany any decision.
questions.answer: Treat the two parts separately and route the second to a clinician. An eye cream applied to the outer periorbital skin is a cosmetic question at the thinnest, most permeable skin on the body, and the claim that it was tested does not address a managed corneal condition, so the product and the question go to the eye-care clinician who can examine the cornea and tear film. Eyeliner at the inner lash line is a different question, because migration across the lid margin has been described and inner-line application is associated with greater tear film contamination and ocular discomfort than application on the outer periocular skin, with makeup removers also shown to increase tear film evaporation. The stop rule is that new eye pain, light sensitivity, discharge, persistent redness or any change in vision means seeking care promptly rather than adjusting a routine.
questions.distractor: A product marked ophthalmologist tested has been assessed for the eye area, so it is suitable despite the corneal condition, and eyeliner at the inner lash line is a stylistic choice because the tear film renews continuously and removes any transferred product.
questions.correction: Site testing establishes tolerance under study conditions in enrolled participants; it does not model a managed corneal condition, does not establish tear-film safety for an individual, and cannot become individualized advice. The tear film is a thin structured layer adjacent to the lid margin, and the evidence describes migration across that margin, greater contamination and discomfort with inner-line application than with outer periocular application, and reduced tear-film stability from makeup removers, most markedly oil-based ones. Nothing in the evidence licenses a self-directed change closest to the ocular surface for someone whose cornea is already under clinical management.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A dermatologist recommends an occlusive ointment for lichenified skin on a shin. The learner dislikes it and asks whether the lighter lotion she prefers delivers the same active, since the percentage on the label is identical. Explain what the vehicle changes, give the site-based reasoning, and include the arithmetic that converts measured delivery into a share of the applied dose.
questions.answer: The percentage is the same and the delivered amount is not. A vehicle changes how available the active is, how much water the stratum corneum holds while the base sits on it, and how long contact lasts, and the vehicle review groups thickened and lichenified skin with the situations where more occlusive bases are preferred. The arithmetic shows the scale: in a 56-compound penetration study using a finite dose of 10 microlitres per square centimetre, delivery ranged from 0.03 to 72.61 micrograms per square centimetre, a factor of about 2,420 between compounds, and if that dose is approximately 10,000 micrograms per square centimetre then the most permeable compound delivered about 0.73 per cent of what was applied while the least delivered about 0.0003 per cent. Consistency of use is the other half of the equation, so the reasonable plan is an occlusive base at night on the thickened area and a preferred lighter product by day, with tolerability treated as part of delivery rather than as vanity.
questions.distractor: The same percentage means the same delivered dose, so the preference for the lotion is legitimate and the dermatologist's recommendation is a matter of texture and habit rather than of formulation science.
questions.correction: Concentration is a property of the product; delivery is a property of the product and the skin together. Occlusion raises hydration and contact time, water resistance extends residence, and fewer preservatives reduce sensitisation risk, which is why the vehicle review associates occlusive bases with glabrous and thickened skin. Measured penetration in a standardised protocol spanned more than three orders of magnitude across compounds and accounted for well under one per cent of the applied dose even at its maximum. Where a clinician has recommended an occlusive base for a thickened site, the productive response is to negotiate how the recommendation is delivered, for example at night, rather than to substitute a base that leaves less active in contact with the skin.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A learner with a history of a rash from a scented body lotion wants to eliminate risk by choosing fragrance-free and paraben-free products, and she wants to know whether that plan is sound. Evaluate the plan using hazard and risk reasoning, the preservative patch-test frequencies, the fragrance labelling rules and the contamination argument.
questions.answer: The plan is partially reasonable and not sufficient. Avoiding a substance that caused a reaction is sensible, but identifying what caused it is a clinical question answerable by patch testing rather than by label avoidance, because fragrances are among the allergen groups reported for periorbital and general contact dermatitis. The preservative data show why a free-from strategy can backfire: in a 50,799-patient series, 22.3 per cent reacted to at least one preservative, methylisothiazolinone reacted in 12.2 per cent and paraben mix in 1 per cent, roughly a twelvefold difference, so removing a paraben says nothing about what replaced it. Fragrance disclosure also limits the plan, since United States rules permit fragrance and flavour ingredients to be listed simply as fragrance to protect trade secrets, so a scented product's sensitiser may be unidentifiable from the label. Finally, a preservative-free, water-containing product carries a contamination argument of its own, since preservation is a consumer-protection function verified by challenge testing and good manufacturing practice, and jar formats opened with fingers add exposure. The sound plan is patch testing, a written avoidance list based on results, and a preference for well-preserved, appropriately packaged, low-fragrance products.
questions.distractor: The plan is sound as written, because removing fragrances and parabens removes the two most common causes of cosmetic contact dermatitis, and preservative-free products avoid both allergy and contamination risk.
questions.correction: The frequency data contradict the second claim: methylisothiazolinone was the most frequent preservative sensitiser in a large patch-test series at 12.2 per cent, while paraben mix was near the bottom at 1 per cent, so a paraben-free choice may move a person to a more frequently sensitising preservative. Fragrance is a legitimate concern, and it is also often unidentifiable from a United States label because the mixture may be declared as fragrance. Preservative-free is not a safety upgrade either, since preservation protects a water-containing product from microbial growth during storage and use, and the relevant quality controls are verified by challenge testing and manufacturing practice rather than by absence of a preservative.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A brand's serum claims to deliver a growth-factor complex that rebuilds collagen, and the cited study measured wrinkle depth at eight weeks in 45 participants with no control group, reporting a 12 per cent relative improvement. A second brand sells a much cheaper matrikine peptide serum and cites a review of products with evidence of skin rejuvenation. Compare the two claims on outcome evidence and mechanism, include the arithmetic, and state what would move either claim into the likely category.
questions.answer: Both claims need separating into measured outcome and stated mechanism. The arithmetic first: 12 per cent of a baseline of 5.0 on a nine-point scale is 0.6 points, which is smaller than typical inter-rater variation on wrinkle severity scales, and with no control group it is also compatible with regression to the mean and behaviour change. The mechanism claim about rebuilding collagen is unsupported by that study, and the review literature notes that growth-factor proteins are poorly penetrating while matrikine and matrikine-like peptides have better penetration because they are much smaller, which if anything favours the cheaper product's plausibility while still not measuring an outcome. What would move either claim to likely is a randomised comparison with a relevant blinded endpoint, a stated duration, an effect exceeding the error of the measurement instrument, and disclosure of funding and interests, since the substantiation standard requires competent and reliable scientific evidence for health-related claims.
questions.distractor: The growth-factor serum is the stronger product because growth factors directly signal collagen synthesis, whereas the matrikine peptide only mimics that activity, so the mechanism difference settles the comparison.
questions.correction: Mechanism plausibility is not outcome evidence, and in this case the mechanism argument runs the other way on delivery. The growth factor review itself states that matrikine and matrikine-like peptides offer growth-factor-like activity with better skin penetration because of their much smaller molecular size, which makes the larger protein complex the less plausible topical candidate, not the stronger one. Neither claim survives on one uncontrolled 45-participant study with a 0.6-point relative change, since a blinded randomised comparison with a relevant endpoint and an effect exceeding measurement error is what the substantiation standard implies for a health-related claim.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A learner wants to buy a microbiome-balancing serum, has 300 dollars a year to spend on skincare, and also reports recurrent stinging on the cheeks and a persistent dry patch on a shin that has not healed in three months. Build the priorities she should follow, including which question is clinical, which interventions have the best evidence behind them, and how to reason about the microbiome claim.
questions.answer: Sort by evidence strength and by clinical urgency. The dry patch that has not healed over three months is a clinical matter and takes priority over any purchase, because a non-healing or changing lesion is a reason to seek assessment rather than to treat cosmetically. The stinging is a tolerability and possibly contact-allergy question, managed by simplifying to a gentle cleanser, a plain emollient and photoprotection, and by seeking patch testing if it persists. The microbiome claim should be filed as preliminary rather than dismissed, since reviews state that the microbiome maintains barrier and homeostasis while evidence for microbiome-targeted cosmetics remains preliminary and microbiome-friendly describes a design intention. With a 300-dollar annual budget, the arithmetic favours the boring interventions: a ceramide or plain emollient moisturiser used generously on the cheeks and the shin will cost a fraction of a premium serum, leaving budget for a broad-spectrum sunscreen, which is the intervention with the strongest evidence in the course.
questions.distractor: Buy the microbiome serum first because it addresses the skin ecosystem underlying both problems, then use the remaining budget on a moisturiser, and treat the dry patch as dryness to be solved with the same routine.
questions.correction: Two errors are combined here. Assigning a non-healing patch to a cosmetic category delays assessment of something that should be seen, which is the masking and delay pattern this course warns about. The second is upgrading preliminary evidence above established evidence: the reviews describe the microbiome as a real system whose commercial targeting remains preliminary, so a microbiome serum cannot be treated as addressing the cause of stinging or of a persistent patch. The defensible plan puts clinical assessment first, keeps the routine minimal and tolerability-focused with a gentle cleanser, emollient and sunscreen, uses patch testing if the stinging persists, and treats the serum as an optional substitution with a written stop rule once the clinical questions are answered.

questions.prompt: Cumulative application. A learner is building her first dossier and asks you to check the seven sections. She has a question, nine sources including four manufacturer brochures, a summary paragraph, a conclusion that the product is worth trying, and a note saying she will stop if it irritates her skin. Diagnose what is missing, state the criteria that should determine her certainty label, and explain the two kinds of stop rule the dossier needs.
questions.answer: Four sections are missing or too vague. The question needs explicit population, intervention, comparison and outcome slots, because without a named comparison the dossier becomes a purchase justification. The sources need rung labels and an appraisal note each, with manufacturer material marked as promotional even when it carries data, and the appraisal template should follow the Cochrane bias domains for trials and a review-level tool for syntheses. The certainty label must be one of likely, uncertain or insufficient chosen by written criteria: likely requires at least one randomised comparison with a relevant outcome and no serious risk-of-bias problem, uncertain means randomised evidence exists but is small, short, inconsistent or indirect, and insufficient means no randomised comparison addresses the endpoint. The cost line is absent and should be computed per year at a stated application volume so products of different sizes can be compared. The stop rule must have two kinds, a tolerance stop for irritation, stinging or new scaling that persists, and a clinical stop for symptoms that belong to a clinician, with anything at the lid margin, lashes or ocular surface routed to an eye-care clinician. A review date and a statement of what would change the decision are also required, since a conclusion that the product is worth trying is a decision with no criteria attached.
questions.distractor: The dossier is essentially complete: nine sources exceed the minimum, the conclusion follows from the evidence gathered, and a single irritation-based stop rule covers the necessary safety element, so the remaining work is cosmetic tidying.
questions.correction: Completeness in a dossier is defined by what the sections make decidable, not by source count. Four of the nine sources being manufacturer brochures matters less than whether they are labelled promotional and appraised; without a comparison slot the question cannot be answered; without criteria a certainty label is a preference; without annual cost arithmetic two differently sized products cannot be compared; and a single irritation stop rule omits the clinical triggers that route symptoms to the right professional. The referral map is not optional in this course, and for a learner with a diagnosed corneal condition the eye-care branch is the one that must never be inferred from a label.

questions.prompt: Cumulative synthesis. A learner presents a plan that uses four products, including a peptide serum, a microbiome serum, an acid exfoliant and an eye area cream applied to the lid margin, justifies each with a mechanism, and reports that she cannot afford a sunscreen. Rebuild the plan using the evidence hierarchy from this level, name the arithmetic that shows where the money should go, and state precisely how the eye-area item changes and why.
questions.answer: Rebuild from evidence strength downward. The strongest evidence in this level supports photoprotection, moisturising with an appropriate vehicle, a gentle cleanser, and a single well-evidenced active trialled one at a time, so the first structural change is to move sunscreen into the plan and treat it as the least negotiable item, since it protects against the process that the other products claim to address. The two mechanism-justified serums should be filed as uncertain or insufficient until a randomised comparison with a relevant blinded endpoint exists, with the peptide review noting limited stratum corneum permeability for a hydrophilic molecule and the microbiome review noting that evidence for microbiome-targeted cosmetics remains preliminary. The exfoliant is a tolerability risk layered on top of stinging, so it goes last or not at all. The arithmetic shows why this ordering frees budget: a product costing 48 dollars for 30 millilitres at 0.5 millilitres twice daily costs 1.60 dollars per millilitre and about 584 dollars a year, while a 50-millilitre product at 22 dollars costs 0.44 dollars per millilitre and about 161 dollars a year, a difference of about 423 dollars that can fund sunscreen and a larger emollient. The eye-area item changes by site and by authority: the lid margin is adjacent to the tear film, migration across the margin has been described, inner-line application is associated with greater tear film contamination and discomfort than outer periocular application, and with a diagnosed corneal condition that area is managed by an eye-care clinician, so the product is either repositioned to the outer periorbital skin under clinical advice or removed from the plan, never applied at the margin.
questions.distractor: Keep the four products because each is supported by a mechanism, add sunscreen when the budget allows, and keep the eye cream as formulated since it is designed for the eye area and the label directions specify the intended site.
questions.correction: Mechanism is the weakest justification in the set: two of the four products rest on mechanisms the literature describes as incompletely understood or preliminary, and the exfoliant adds an unnecessary tolerability risk to a plan that already reports stinging. The budget arithmetic is the decisive point, because the annual difference between a premium serum and a mid-priced equivalent is large enough to fund the intervention with the strongest evidence in the course, and sunscreen is not a discretionary addition when the other products claim to address photoaging. The eye-area reasoning fails on both site and authority: the lid margin is contiguous with the tear film, migration across it has been described, inner-line application has been associated with greater tear film contamination than outer application, and a diagnosed corneal condition places decisions in that region with an eye-care clinician rather than with a label.
